headline: US midterms: Michigan Democrat's endorsement of Republican ruffles critical Senate race
description: Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens, who lost the Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly ‌contested race, publicly backs Republican Mike Rogers.
author: Reuters
article_text:
A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in ​a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.

US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly ‌contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.

“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media.

Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party. He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country.”

Thirty-five Senate seats and ​all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favored to win a majority of the House and are locked in a ​tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.

If Democrats take control of the House or ⁠Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.

The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda ​without the aid of Congress, including its tarrif pressure on trading partners.

Michigan rift

Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called ​on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.

“That ad was very painful,” Stevens told CNN on Sunday night. “There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’”

El-Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said.

Republicans sought to capitalise ​on Stevens’ move. “This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said. “When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of ​people, it gets dangerous.”

Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” - attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.

Stevens’ move did not appear to dent support ‌for El-Sayed. A ⁠New York Times/Siena poll released and partly conducted on Sunday showed the Democratic nominee with a 53 per cent to 42pc lead over Rogers.

A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign said that it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers, making it the campaign’s second-best fundraising day since the Democratic primary election in August.

He declined to directly address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday.

“This race was never about me,” El-Sayed told MS NOW. “It was never even about Mike Rogers. It’s certainly not about Haley Stevens. This race is about the people in the state of Michigan, the people that I’ve gotten to know in their churches and synagogues, in their basements and their living rooms, talking about what they need and deserve.”

A number of ​Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to ​reports from CNN and the Hill, while some voters expressed ⁠disdain.

“Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after casting her ballot for El-Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.

Alaska Intervention Falters

Also on Sunday, the Trump administration’s attempt to intervene in Alaska’s Senate race faltered when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly ​loses.

The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr on the same ballot.

The issue has roiled the campaign ​over the last several days after ⁠the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr into the race as a spoiler.

The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday’s election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue. But Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola, and the incumbent Sullivan declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification.

He joined his party colleagues in accusing ⁠the other Sullivan ​of trying to confuse voters with his similar name.

“They got the decoy guy on the ballot,” the senator told CNN’s “State of the Union” ​program. “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, ‘Don’t let them get away with the tricks.”

Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.

article_html:
A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in ​a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.

US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly ‌contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.

“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media.

Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party. He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country.”

Thirty-five Senate seats and ​all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favored to win a majority of the House and are locked in a ​tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.

If Democrats take control of the House or ⁠Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.

The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda ​without the aid of Congress, including its tarrif pressure on trading partners.

Michigan rift

Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called ​on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.

“That ad was very painful,” Stevens told CNN on Sunday night. “There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’”

El-Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said.

Republicans sought to capitalise ​on Stevens’ move. “This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said. “When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of ​people, it gets dangerous.”

Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” - attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.

Stevens’ move did not appear to dent support ‌for El-Sayed. A ⁠New York Times/Siena poll released and partly conducted on Sunday showed the Democratic nominee with a 53 per cent to 42pc lead over Rogers.

A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign said that it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers, making it the campaign’s second-best fundraising day since the Democratic primary election in August.

He declined to directly address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday.

“This race was never about me,” El-Sayed told MS NOW. “It was never even about Mike Rogers. It’s certainly not about Haley Stevens. This race is about the people in the state of Michigan, the people that I’ve gotten to know in their churches and synagogues, in their basements and their living rooms, talking about what they need and deserve.”

A number of ​Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to ​reports from CNN and the Hill, while some voters expressed ⁠disdain.

“Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after casting her ballot for El-Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.

Alaska Intervention Falters

Also on Sunday, the Trump administration’s attempt to intervene in Alaska’s Senate race faltered when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly ​loses.

The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr on the same ballot.

The issue has roiled the campaign ​over the last several days after ⁠the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr into the race as a spoiler.

The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday’s election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue. But Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola, and the incumbent Sullivan declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification.

He joined his party colleagues in accusing ⁠the other Sullivan ​of trying to confuse voters with his similar name.

“They got the decoy guy on the ballot,” the senator told CNN’s “State of the Union” ​program. “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, ‘Don’t let them get away with the tricks.”

Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.

headline: Is cooking oil really the problem? Dr Yousuf Kamal Mirza explains 5 things every consumer should look for
description: The key is understanding which fats to choose and what to look for in the cooking oil we use every day.
author: ADVERTORIAL
article_text:
Cooking oil is an essential part of our everyday meals. From preparing breakfast to cooking family favourites, it plays an important role in our food and kitchens. Yet, many people tend to associate cooking oil with health concerns, often overlooking the fact that the type and quality of oil we consume also matter.

According to Dr Yousuf Kamal Mirza, Senior Consultant Physician at Aga Khan University Hospital and Tabba Heart and Medilink Clinics, fats, just like carbohydrates, proteins and vitamins, are an integral part of our health. The key is understanding which fats to choose and what to look for in the cooking oil we use every day, he also emphasises that choosing a cooking oil should go beyond taste, price and everyday convenience. Consumers should pay attention to its nutritional composition, quality and performance during cooking.

Dr Mirza highlights five important considerations when selecting cooking oil:

Zero Cholesterol and Unsaturated Fats: Choose cooking oils that are cholesterol-free and contain unsaturated fats, including monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, as important nutritional attributes to consider when making informed choices for everyday cooking and supports heart health“
Omega 3 and Omega 6: Essential fatty acids that support normal bodily functions.
Vitamins A, D and E: Important fat-soluble vitamins that contribute to various bodily functions.
Less Oil Absorption: An important consideration for the amount of oil absorbed by food during cooking.
High Quality Refining: An essential factor in the quality of cooking oil.

Interestingly, these five considerations come together in Mezan 5 PRO, featuring Omega 3 and 6, Vitamins A, D & E, Zero Cholesterol, Less Oil Absorption and High Quality Refining.

So, perhaps the question isn’t whether cooking oil belongs in our food, but whether we are choosing the right cooking oil for our everyday meals.

headline: Iran says considering two-day plan to reopen Hormuz
description: Iran’s foreign ministry said it was considering a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US agrees to...
article_text:
Iran’s foreign ministry said it was considering a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US agrees to its conditions, having previously proposed a one-week timeline, Reuters reports.

“The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran’s good-faith approach. We have stated that, if Iran’s demands are met, it would be possible to restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and resume the negotiating process within a short period,” said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei, adding that the “exchange of messages is still ongoing” via mediators.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz are all feasible if the United States demonstrates goodwill, has a genuine willingness to reach an agreement, and truly seeks a peaceful solution.

In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi said a proposal currently under discussion through Qatari and Pakistani mediation was based on Iran’s original seven-day plan, which Tehran presented during the UN General Assembly in New York in September.

Under the initial plan, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the sixth day if Iran’s conditions were met, and Iran-US negotiations would resume on the seventh day, according to Araghchi.

He said continued consultations among Iranian, Qatari, and Pakistani officials helped make the proposal more practical. A Qatari suggestion to shorten the seven-day timeline had led to a new two-day plan.

headline: Araghchi says US must lift sanctions, end blockade for Hormuz reopening
description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran now expects Washington to lift the new sanctions imposed after the...
article_text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran now expects Washington to lift the new sanctions imposed after the memorandum, scale back its military presence in the region to its previous level, end the blockade and implement the planned waivers on oil sanctions.

“There is nothing extraordinary about these conditions, and all of them are feasible if the US side demonstrates goodwill, has a genuine will to reach an agreement, and is truly seeking a peaceful solution,” Araghchi said.

He said the proposal could pave the way for peace, restore normal traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and help return life to normal in the region and beyond.

Araghchi said reopening the strategic waterway would be followed by negotiations on issues of mutual interest. Iran wants to negotiate the complete lifting of sanctions, while the United States is interested in discussing the nuclear issue, he added.

headline: UAE state oil company announces OpenAI partnership
description: Says OpenAI’s models will analyse decades of data from thousands of wells and hundreds of facilities to prepare and optimise oilfield development plans.
author: AFP
article_text:
UAE state oil company ADNOC on Monday announced a partnership with OpenAI, saying it would be the world’s first energy firm to deploy OpenAI Frontier, an advanced artificial intelligence platform.

The deal was announced as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman attended the UAE’s flagship oil industry event in Abu Dhabi, which has bet heavily on the technology in a bid to diversify its economy away from energy.

Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, but the US military has been escorting ships through the route.

The blockade has caused a spike in oil prices.

ADNOC said in a statement that OpenAI’s models will enable it to be “the first energy company in the world to use this technology to value every barrel while it is still in the ground”.

The deal will also see ADNOC and OpenAI partner with G42, and Emirati AI company chaired by the brother of the UAE’s president.

The oil-rich UAE is a top AI player in the Middle East and has been seeking to become a dominant force in the field globally.

“From the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI, and now together we will find out what AI can do for energy,” said ADNOC’s managing director and CEO Sultan Al Jaber at the ADIPEC oil conference.

Altman praised the UAE as having “consistently been the most forward-looking country in the world for AI adoption”.

According to an ADNOC statement, “OpenAI’s advanced reasoning models will integrate decades of data across thousands of wells, multiple stacked reservoirs and hundreds of surface facilities together with capital, cost and commercial considerations, to prepare and optimise full-field development master plans”.

“Interconnected AI agents will continuously forecast crude oil supply, demand, prices and margins, predict their impacts before they occur, and weigh the commercial and operational impact of every decision as one integrated process,” the statement said.

No financial details of the deal were disclosed.

The UAE has been betting heavily on AI since 2017, when it named the world’s first AI minister and became the second country after Canada to unveil a national AI strategy.

A year later, G42 was founded with backing from Abu Dhabi-based sovereign wealth fund Mubadala. Chaired by the UAE president’s brother, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, it offers a range of AI products and employs more than 23,000 people.

Last year, intense lobbying bore fruit when the US approved the export of advanced Nvidia chips to both the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

On Sunday, Saudi state oil firm Aramco said it was taking a 49 percent stake in Saudi state-backed AI company Humain, injecting cash and assets as the tech firm tries to scale up to meet rising demand.

Aramco, one of the world’s biggest companies by market capitalisation, will inject about 9.9 billion Saudi riyals ($2.6bn) into Humain this year along with AI, compute and digital assets.

The UAE has been betting heavily on AI since 2017, when it named the world’s first AI minister and became the second country after Canada to unveil a national AI strategy.

A year later, G42 was founded with backing from Abu Dhabi-based sovereign wealth fund Mubadala. Chaired by the UAE president’s brother, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, it offers a range of AI products and employs more than 23,000 people.
Last year, intense lobbying bore fruit when the US approved the export of advanced Nvidia chips to both the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

On Sunday, Saudi state oil firm Aramco said it was taking a 49 percent stake in Saudi state-backed AI company Humain, injecting cash and assets as the tech firm tries to scale up to meet rising demand.
Aramco, one of the world’s biggest companies by market capitalisation, will inject about 9.9 billion Saudi riyals ($2.6bn) into Humain this year along with AI, compute and digital assets.

headline: China's foreign minister pushes for dialogue to resolve Middle East conflict
description: China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi said that all parties in the Middle East conflict should focus on political...

China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi said that all parties in the Middle East conflict should focus on political solutions rather than resorting to arms again, in a meeting with an Iranian national security official in Beijing, Reuters reports.

Dialogue and negotiation are the way to resolve Middle East conflicts, Wang said to Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of the Iran Supreme National Security Council, according to Chinese state new agency Xinhua.

Wang also said China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security.

headline: Laden with eggs, robots race up sacred Chinese mountain
description: Cover over 3,000 steps up Mount Tai.
author: AFP
article_text:
Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China’s most famous peaks on Monday, carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organisers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.

For hundreds of years, Mount Tai — the tallest peak in China’s eastern Shandong province — was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors and features prominently in Chinese mythology.

But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.

The Unesco World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.

Over a 3.9-kilometre course with more than 600 metres of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods like fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.

A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology — a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree — completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.

Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.

The fastest humanoid robot — belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue — completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.

Organisers called Mount Tai’s rocky terrain a “natural extreme testing ground” that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.

The race, organised by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

headline: Bangladesh garment workers protesting for higher wages clash with police
description: Protesters demand 30,000-taka monthly wage; police fire stun grenades, tear gas canisters to disperse crowds in Ashulia, the site of some of the country's largest factories.
author: AFP
article_text:
Thousands of Bangladeshi garment workers blocked a major highway and clashed with police on Monday, demanding a monthly minimum wage more than double their current pay, as protests spread across industrial hubs.

The South Asian nation of 170 million people is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, manufacturing clothes for some of the largest international brands.

Hundreds of workers in Gazipur, north of the capital Dhaka, blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, vandalising several vehicles, while large groups took to the streets in the Mirpur district, where police dispersed demonstrators with tear gas, AFP reporters saw.

Angry workers also set fire to a police vehicle.

The protests came despite the government’s announcement on Sunday that it would establish a wage board to review the minimum wage in the vital garment industry, which employs millions of people and generates the bulk of Bangladesh’s export earnings.

However, labour leaders say workers’ grievances extend beyond the formation of the board, citing inflation and rising household expenses.

The protesters demand a 30,000-taka monthly wage, more than double their current pay.

Workers currently earn about 13,000 taka a month, according to Kalpona Akter of the Bangladesh Centre for Workers Solidarity.

Police fired stun grenades and tear gas canisters to disperse crowds in Ashulia, a Dhaka suburb and the site of some of the country’s largest factories.

“Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up — the government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages,” said Mamum, 28, a factory worker.

Machine operator Sharmin, 24, said: “We keep the wheels of the economy turning. They must listen to us.” Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned that the government was taking strong action to stop the protests.

“Those engaging in unlawful activities and conspiracies under the guise of labour movements will be tackled with an iron hand,” he said after meeting industry leaders on Monday.

‘Crack down’

However, Ahmed also said earlier Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had instructed officials after hosting an emergency cabinet meeting late on Sunday to “ensure workers’ rights and improve their living standards”.

He said Rahman had told them to make sure production and exports continued “unhindered”.

Bangladesh’s main manufacturer associations for garments and knitwear warned that “prolonged unrest could disrupt production, delay export shipments and affect Bangladesh’s commitments to international buyers”, the state-run BSS news agency said on Monday.

Kamrul Hasan, general secretary of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, told AFP some labour leaders had gone into hiding.

“We were not prepared for this unrest either, as the wage board has already been formed,” he said.

“But workers are now protesting over wages and other unresolved issues.”

In Ashulia, security officers chased protesters as they scattered down narrow side streets, with the choking tear gas drifting into densely packed housing where families often live crammed into single rooms.

“Police fired tear gas shells inside our compound,” said Kamona, 24, who gave only one name.

“We have children, but they don’t care.”

Industry representatives said workers from at least 529 factories in Dhaka and its surrounding industrial areas, including Savar, Ashulia, Jirani and Gazipur, had left their workplaces on Sunday.

The South Asian nation of 170 million people is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, manufacturing clothes for some of the largest international brands.

Hundreds of workers in Gazipur, north of the capital Dhaka, blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, vandalising several vehicles, while large groups took to the streets in the Mirpur district, where police dispersed demonstrators with tear gas, AFP reporters saw.
Angry workers also set fire to a police vehicle.

The protests came despite the government’s announcement on Sunday that it would establish a wage board to review the minimum wage in the vital garment industry, which employs millions of people and generates the bulk of Bangladesh’s export earnings.
However, labour leaders say workers’ grievances extend beyond the formation of the board, citing inflation and rising household expenses.
The protesters demand a 30,000-taka monthly wage, more than double their current pay.
Workers currently earn about 13,000 taka a month, according to Kalpona Akter of the Bangladesh Centre for Workers Solidarity.
Police fired stun grenades and tear gas canisters to disperse crowds in Ashulia, a Dhaka suburb and the site of some of the country’s largest factories.
“Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up — the government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages,” said Mamum, 28, a factory worker.

Machine operator Sharmin, 24, said: “We keep the wheels of the economy turning. They must listen to us.” Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned that the government was taking strong action to stop the protests.
“Those engaging in unlawful activities and conspiracies under the guise of labour movements will be tackled with an iron hand,” he said after meeting industry leaders on Monday.
‘Crack down’

However, Ahmed also said earlier Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had instructed officials after hosting an emergency cabinet meeting late on Sunday to “ensure workers’ rights and improve their living standards”.
He said Rahman had told them to make sure production and exports continued “unhindered”.

Bangladesh’s main manufacturer associations for garments and knitwear warned that “prolonged unrest could disrupt production, delay export shipments and affect Bangladesh’s commitments to international buyers”, the state-run BSS news agency said on Monday.
Kamrul Hasan, general secretary of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, told AFP some labour leaders had gone into hiding.
“We were not prepared for this unrest either, as the wage board has already been formed,” he said.
“But workers are now protesting over wages and other unresolved issues.”

In Ashulia, security officers chased protesters as they scattered down narrow side streets, with the choking tear gas drifting into densely packed housing where families often live crammed into single rooms.
“Police fired tear gas shells inside our compound,” said Kamona, 24, who gave only one name.
“We have children, but they don’t care.”
Industry representatives said workers from at least 529 factories in Dhaka and its surrounding industrial areas, including Savar, Ashulia, Jirani and Gazipur, had left their workplaces on Sunday.

headline: Saudi Arabia briefly activates emergency alerts in 3 cities amid hostilities with Yemen’s Houthis

article_text:
Saudi Arabia briefly activated emergency alerts in the southwestern cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait and Taif in the country’s west before later announcing that the danger had passed in the three areas, Anadolu reports.

The warnings were issued through the National Early Warning Platform for Emergencies, according to separate statements by the Saudi Civil Defence.

It later announced that the danger had passed in Abha, Khamis Mushait and Taif, and urged residents to continue following Civil Defense instructions and avoid gathering or filming.

headline: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says

article_text:
Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States, ​and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting ‌possible, an official briefed on the talks said, Reuters reports.

The negotiators departed on Sunday, though not because of difficulties in the negotiations, the official said, without providing further details on the ​draft proposal.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the basis of the talks is ​a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the ⁠Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran, with Tehran ​now suggesting that proposal could be implemented on a faster timeline under a deal.

headline: Oil drops over 4pc on hopes of progress in talks on ending US-Iran war
description: Oil fell more than 4 per cent as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials on a deal to end the US-Israeli war on...
article_text:
Oil fell more than 4 per cent as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials on a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran raised hopes that Middle East supply disruptions could ease, Reuters reports.

Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States, and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said on Monday.

“The new month brought with it renewed hopes of a breakthrough in the Iranian stalemate,” said Tamas Varga of oil broker PVM.

Brent crude futures fell $4.79, or 4.2pc, to $108.64 a barrel by 1020 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude traded at $99.71, down $4.41 or 4.2pc.

headline: Babar, Shaheen set for Quaid-e-Azam Trophy opening-round clash
description: Babar will turn out for Lahore Whites, who face Shaheen-led Fata at the Diamond Cricket Ground in Islamabad, in what promises to be one of the early highlights of the premier first-class competition.
author: Dawn Sport
article_text:
Pakistan Test captain Babar Azam and One-day International skipper Shaheen Shah Afridi will headline the opening round of the 69th edition of the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy, which gets under way across Islamabad, Abbottabad and Rawalpindi on Tuesday.

Babar will turn out for Lahore Whites, who face Shaheen-led Fata at the Diamond Cricket Ground in Islamabad, in what promises to be one of the early highlights of the premier first-class competition.

Several other established Pakistan players will also feature in the tournament, with Saud Shakeel captaining defending champions Karachi Blues, Mohammad Rizwan leading Peshawar Blues and Imam-ul-Haq taking charge of Multan. Abdullah Shafique will captain Sialkot Blues, while Mohammad Nawaz has been named skipper of Rawalpindi in the Silver tier.

The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Monday announced the schedule and team rosters for the Gold and Silver competitions, which will run simultaneously and feature 20 regional sides.

Eight teams will compete in the Gold tier, with Karachi Blues, Faisalabad, Fata, Lahore Whites, Islamabad, Peshawar Blues, Multan and Sialkot Blues vying for the title. The competition will run from Nov 3 to Dec 12, with the five-day final scheduled for Dec 15-19.

The winners will be crowned champions of the 69th edition of the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy, while the 12-team Silver competition will provide a pathway to the top tier for next season.

The Silver teams have been divided into two groups of six. Lahore Blues, Rawalpindi, Larkana, Quetta, Bahawalpur and Peshawar Whites form Group ‘A’, while Group ‘B’ comprises Karachi Whites, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Hyderabad, Dera Murad Jamali, Abbottabad and Sialkot Whites.

Group ‘A’ matches will be staged at the KCCA Stadium, SBP and UBL Sports Complexes in Karachi, while Group ‘B’ fixtures will be held at the Multan Cricket Stadium, Sports Complex in Rahim Yar Khan and Dring Stadium in Bahawalpur.

The Silver group matches will take place from Nov 3-30, with the final between the two group winners scheduled for Dec 3-7. The winners will earn promotion to the Gold tier for the following season.

A total of 60 first-class matches will be played across the two competitions, with 29 fixtures in Gold and 31 in Silver. Both tiers will carry first-class status.

The tournament will also mark the first time that Peshawar and Sialkot regions will field two teams each in a first-class competition.

In the Gold tier, Lahore Whites’ squad includes Babar, all-rounder Aamir Jamal, Tayyab Tahir and Noman Ali, while Fata will be led by Shaheen and also feature Khushdil Shah and Mohammad Wasim Khan.

Karachi Blues, meanwhile, have retained a strong line-up under Saud, with Saim Ayub and Omair Bin Yousuf among the players in their squad. Shan Masood, Abrar Ahmed and Mir Hamza are included in the team’s reserves and national-duty pool.

Peshawar Blues will be captained by wicket-keeper batter Rizwan, with Sahibzada Farhan, Mohammad Haris and Iftikhar Ahmed also named in the squad.

In the Silver competition, Abbottabad have included Fakhar Zaman and Kamran Ghulam, while Rawalpindi’s squad features Shadab Khan, Haider Ali, Mohammad Nawaz and Jahandad Khan.

The PCB said teams would operate with revolving rosters throughout the tournament, with 15 travelling members and the option to draw on reserve players and those in the national-duty pool when available.

headline: Dear Test cricket, I stayed up
description: A love letter to Test cricket, exploring its beauty, uncertainty and humanity through a five-day drama featuring South Africa and Australia in Cape Town.
author: Junaid Aziz
article_text:
Newlands, Cape Town. Saturday morning, before the first ball.

Marnus Labuschagne crouches on his haunches at the edge of the outfield, waiting to bat. Australia need 288 to win the Test and the series. In the first innings he made a five-ball duck. He has scored 11 Test hundreds, and the last came at Old Trafford in July 2023. For a stretch he was the best batter in the world.

He stands, walks to the middle, and takes guard. He will face three balls. I have not stopped thinking about them.

Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write…

Chapter One: Moved

Some months earlier

I write about this game only when it moves me. Good cricket does not count. Good cricket arrives every week and asks nothing of you. Being moved is rarer: a stranger does something you did not know a person could do, in a country you may never see, at an hour when you should be asleep, and for a few minutes you stop being an audience and become a witness. The first Test of the Ashes did that to me, in two days, and I wrote about it. I watched the other four to the last ball. Then the series ended, an English summer came and went, and I could not name you one innings. Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write, and the universe, with its usual disregard for my sleep, took the job. My resistance lasted about one session.

Chapter Two: Two Rooms

Same city. Same Saturday night

In the first room, a performer who has done this show 200 times walks onto a stage built for it. The lighting is rehearsed. The song you came for arrives second, exactly where it was promised. The audience paid for that, and it is delivered to the minute. Nobody leaves disappointed and nobody leaves changed. This is entertainment, and I have nothing against it. Its virtue is that it keeps its word.

In the second room, a band walks out with sketches and no plan. In the spring of 1959 Miles Davis brought his musicians into a studio with little more than a handful of scales and melodic outlines, and what they made became the best-selling jazz record of all time. It could have been a mess. The patron in that room knows it could have been a mess, because he has sat through the nights when it was. He pays for the chance to find out.

The two audiences differ in more than taste. The first judges the evening against a promise. The second judges himself against the evening: was I paying enough attention to be there when it happened? Entertainment asks whether you enjoyed it. Art asks whether you were awake.

Test cricket is the second room, stretched to five days.

Chapter Three: Tuesday

Newlands, day one

The series stands at one all. Australia won in Durban by 214, on Matt Renshaw’s 190. South Africa won in Gqeberha by an innings and 31 runs, on Temba Bavuma’s 179. Cape Town decides it.

Pat Cummins wins the toss and chooses to field, citing moisture in the pitch. A captain has made that choice at Newlands only 12 times since 1889. The moisture turns out to be a rumour. By lunch Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram have South Africa at 140 without loss.

Ackerman is playing his second Test. He makes 95 off 94 balls, with twelve fours and two sixes, four of the fours in a row off Mitchell Starc. Then, five runs short of a hundred, he walks down the pitch to Nathan Lyon, who has waited 15 years for that look on a batter’s face. Stumped. Afterward Ackerman says he lives by the sword and dies by it, and that he left a hundred out there. He does not pretend to be happy about it.

Then Starc.

There is a kind of bowler around whom an afternoon changes ownership. Wasim Akram is one. Shane Warne was another. The scoreboard was never the evidence. The evidence was the batter, who knew first. On Tuesday evening Starc joins them. He has Bedingham caught on 50 and, two balls later, Wiaan Mulder, caught behind for a duck. He takes Rickelton and Jansen in a single over with the new ball, then Coetzee and Rabada. South Africa fall from 203 for 1 to 329 all out. Starc finishes with six for 72, his 20th five-wicket haul, and he is not done.

Mulder walks off with a zero beside his name. Keep that number.

In the last half hour of the day Starc is bowling himself off his feet, and at the start of his 22nd over he reaches down for his right calf and runs in anyway.

Chapter Four: Wednesday

Day two

Simon Harmer has Travis Head chopping on for 41. Then Labuschagne, going back to a ball that wanted him forward, edges it to slip, where Aiden Markram takes the catch. Five balls. No runs. He arrived at Newlands needing a score to keep his place, and Australia are 58 for 2.

Tuesday, Mulder: nought. Wednesday, Labuschagne: nought. The match sets them side by side and says nothing.

I am travelling, and the Test starts at an hour that my body, wherever it thinks it is, cannot place. By the second night I have moved two meetings. By the fourth I have moved the rest. I, who could not spare 10 minutes for cricket since the Ashes, now discover that I have five days.

Chapter Five: Friday

Day four

Thursday belongs to Australia. Josh Inglis makes 102 off 135 balls and, with Alex Carey, who makes 80, adds 185. Australia lead by 100. By the close South Africa are four down and 40 ahead, a lead you could carry in one hand.

Friday belongs to two men who have known each other since school. Ryan Rickelton already owns a Test double century and is still the quieter name in a batting order that includes Aiden Markram and Temba Bavuma. Mulder walked off on Tuesday with a zero.

Their plan is a lesson in humility. Rickelton has decided to take a few on the body rather than play the short ball, and he does. He spends 37 balls in the 90s. On 92, Starc bangs one in short, Rickelton shoulders arms, and it thuds into his ribs. He lifts his shirt to show Travis Head, at short leg, the bruise coming up, for confirmation or approval. Head, by all accounts, offers both.

Rickelton reaches his hundred after tea and finishes on 101 off 219 balls. Then Mulder reverse-sweeps, Josh Inglis dives at backward point to cut it off, and Rickelton is run out, the stumps broken by Labuschagne. The stand is worth 154.

It would be easier to say that Mulder rescued South Africa. What he does is odder. He rescues himself, and South Africa happens to be standing next to him. He makes 115 off 221 balls, and on the stroke of stumps he clubs Cummins to deep midwicket, where Mitchell Starc, who has done everything else on this ground for three days, takes the catch. South Africa have 387. Australia need 288.

Wiaan Mulder. Tuesday: 0. Friday: 115.

The same 387 would have been a decent total on Tuesday. On Friday, on a pitch that has begun to come apart, from a side that was four down the night before, it is a verdict.

Nothing else in sport asks you to be brave slowly, and then makes you wait through the night to learn whether it counted.

Chapter Six: Saturday Morning

Day five

Kagiso Rabada has the new ball. Travis Head takes a single off the second delivery. The third is down the leg side, Matt Renshaw, the hero of Durban, is strangled, and Rickelton takes the catch behind the stumps. A golden duck. Labuschagne gets up off his haunches and walks out.

David Warner had predicted that the day would end with Labuschagne a 100 not out and Australia winning with seven wickets down.

The first ball Marnus faces runs off the leading edge, past gully, for four. Two balls later Rabada bowls one that nips back. Labuschagne, playing no shot, is hit on the back pad in front of the stumps. Richard Kettleborough raises his finger. Labuschagne reviews. The replay shows the ball clipping the off bail, which makes it umpire’s call, and the original decision stands. Out for four. 5-2.

Umpire’s call is a rule written for doubt. If the ball is only clipping the stump, the umpire’s original decision stands, whatever it was. Had Kettleborough shaken his head, the very same replay would have left Labuschagne standing where he was.

I have thought about the innings that follows that headshake more than I have thought about most of the ones that were played. It starts the way his best always have, quietly: a leave, a leave, a punch through cover that sounds like a door closing on a bad year.

By lunch he is on 30, and Australia, three down, are breathing again. By tea the drought is over. By the close it is a hundred, and Warner’s forecast, which sounded absurd that morning, looks like prophecy. It never happened. I would swear I watched it.

This is what faith costs in Test cricket, and what luck pays out. Everything Labuschagne has done since he was a boy, the dawn nets, the leaves, the belief, is weighed in the end against a sliver of bail and one man’s reading of it.

Luck is not the opposite of skill in this game. It is the second signature on the contract. A batter can prepare for everything except the sliver, and the sliver is where Test cricket keeps its mystery.

I wrote once about Virat Kohli and the fifth stump, that line outside off where a ball extends an invitation and a great batter accepts it against his own training.

Kohli was beaten by the ball he should have left. Labuschagne was beaten by the ball he left. The craft is the same and so is the verdict: the sport does not care how well you prepared. I support South Africa. I have rarely been so sorry to see them succeed.

By the end of the day Nathan Lyon, at number 10, will have made 33 not out, the top score of the innings, 29 more than a man who was once the best batter in the world.

Labuschagne has the application, the talent, the faith and the hours. All of it is still there. And one morning, for no reason anyone can name, it leaves, the way a word does when you say it too many times and it becomes a sound. He may have played his last Test for Australia in that over. I hope not.

Marnus Labuschagne. Wednesday: 0. Saturday: 4.

Head scores the way a vending machine dispenses: promptly, correctly, and without looking at you. He hits a few boundaries, then edges Rabada to Marco Jansen at gully. 14. It is Rabada’s 350th Test wicket, reached in 13,808 balls, faster than any bowler in history and 911 balls quicker than Dale Steyn. I am alarmed by how much I enjoy it.

Simon Harmer comes on in the 12th over, and the morning comes apart. Inglis is run out for four after Cameron Green sets off for a run that was never on, and Ackerman, who left a hundred on the field on Tuesday, takes a wicket back from silly point.

Alex Carey reverse-sweeps and top-edges to Jansen. Cooper Connolly is caught behind for nought. Starc, promoted to number eight to deal with the footmarks, survives 25 balls without scoring and is caught at bat-pad off the last ball before lunch, the longest duck of his Test career. At lunch Australia are 60 for 7. Harmer has 3-5 from eight overs.

Chapter Seven: Saturday Afternoon

Day five, after lunch.

After lunch the match stops moving, and it becomes the best thing in it. Australia score two runs in an hour. There is a stretch of 78 balls without a run. Green is sheltered from Harmer’s off breaks, and Cummins, who has come out beside him with a plan to bat time instead of runs, defends everything that comes.

Six fielders crouch around the bat. It is a standoff in which the only weapon anyone holds is patience. When the first run finally comes, the Newlands crowd cheers it, ironically and at length. Then Harmer changes ends, drags one through Green’s gate, and Green is bowled for 27. 62-8.

And then two men who have no business being dangerous become dangerous. Cummins faces 90 balls and scores 11 runs, and I have never been prouder of a ratio. Nathan Lyon, who bowled 44 overs in South Africa’s second innings, bats as though that were a warm-up. They add 45. The result was settled hours ago. They know it, the crowd knows it, and everyone awake across the world knows it. They stay anyway.

This is the strange, magnificent design of the thing. A Test match asks the athlete to bring his best courage and his best stamina not for an hour but for five days. Then, on the fifth afternoon, when the specialists have failed, it hands the match to the people who were hired to do something else.

A fast bowler walks out and decides to become a wall. A spinner decides to become a clock. Nothing they do will change the result, and that is exactly why it matters. A win is a fact. This is a gift.

When a man spends 90 balls on something that cannot be won, the scoreboard stops being the point, and the rest of us find out what valour looks like once the reward has been taken away.

Just before tea Harmer traps Cummins lbw. Cummins reviews. The ball is clipping the off bail, and the umpire’s call stands. It is the second time that day those words have decided a man’s fate, and both times the call goes South Africa’s way.

Every great Test victory owes something to luck. Then, with the first ball of his 22nd over, Harmer bowls Josh Hazlewood. Australia are all out for 111. South Africa win by 176.

Harmer finishes with 6 for 16 from 21.1 overs, 14 of them maidens, and 10 wickets in the match, the first time he has done that in a Test. He is 37. He bowled through a torn nail on Thursday. He spent years with Essex in English county cricket, was recalled, and on a Saturday in Cape Town takes apart the top-ranked Test side in the world.

Chapter Eight: Everyone Awake

Some hours later.

A machine can give you the result of this Test in one line. It will be correct, and it will take four seconds. Australia 111, South Africa by 176, the series 2-1.

It cannot tell you what it was like to be awake for it.

We are living through a strange subtraction. Answers arrive before the questions are finished. Summaries sit above the thing they summarise. Almost everything that once cost an afternoon now costs a tap, and the cost was never the enemy.

The cost was where the meaning was kept. A letter mattered because it took a week. A song mattered because you had to wait for the radio to play it. Take away the wait and you take away the room where the feeling lived.

Test cricket is the last large public thing built so that nothing can be skipped. You cannot fast-forward the 90th ball. You cannot be told how it felt. The only way to know is to stay, and staying is the whole price of admission, paid in the oldest currency we have: hours, spent in company.

Somewhere in that fifth afternoon, in a time zone that had no business being awake, a stranger was watching Cummins defend a ball for a reason no efficiency expert would accept. Most of us had no stake in the result. We were there because the sport asks a very human question, which is whether you will stay.

That is human-centred design. The game is built to the scale of a person. It takes five days because a person needs five days to become who he will be on the fifth. It lets a man fail in public and return in the second innings.

It makes 10 team-mates watch each member be afraid, one at a time, and know exactly what it costs. And in an age that can produce the likeness of almost anything, it offers the one thing that cannot be produced: a reason to stay up with strangers for something that may not end well, and to be glad you did.

Chapter Nine: Thank You

16 months earlier, and also now.

In June 2025 I sat at Lord’s through Rabada’s third-innings spell of the World Test Championship final and watched Bavuma lift the mace. It was South Africa’s first global title in 27 years, and it was the day and the occasion that moved me most that year.

That same summer I wrote about a five-Test series and called the piece Five Shades of Flat. Now the same South Africans, under Bavuma, who lost the first Test of this series and won the next two, are the number one Test side in the world for the first time since January 2016.

Thank you Test Cricket..

Thank you For lunch, to begin with, which stops a Test match at its most dangerous moment so that twenty-two men can have a civilized meal.

For tea, the second truce of the day.

For the maiden over, the only unit of achievement in sport defined by nothing happening.

For the duck, a zero named after a bird, so that even the worst day a batter can have arrives with a little feathered mercy.

For a game in which a man can score eleven in ninety balls and be remembered as a hero, and another can score four in three balls and be mourned.

For umpire’s call, in which a machine admits it is not sure.

For the nightwatchman, the bad light, the follow-on, the draw that feels like a victory and the victory that feels like a funeral.

We could not have invented you. No committee would have approved you. You take five days to say what other sports say in two hours, and you say it better, because you leave room for people to be wrong in public and the time for them to come back.

I closed the laptop. The room was quiet, and the quiet was full, the way a house is after the guests have gone. Whether Marnus Labuschagne walks out again for Australia is the one thing this match left unanswered. Test cricket will answer in its own time. I intend to be awake when it does.

Yours, awake.. I suspect he is too.

Newlands, Cape Town. Saturday morning, before the first ball.

Marnus Labuschagne crouches on his haunches at the edge of the outfield, waiting to bat. Australia need 288 to win the Test and the series. In the first innings he made a five-ball duck. He stands, walks to the middle, and takes guard. He will face three balls. I have not stopped thinking about them.

Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write…

Part One: The Wait

Chapter One: Moved

Some months earlier

I write about this game only when it moves me. Good cricket does not count. Good cricket arrives every week and asks nothing of you. Being moved is rarer: a stranger does something you did not know a person could do, in a country you may never see, at an hour when you should be asleep, and for a few minutes you stop being an audience and become a witness. The first Test of the Ashes did that to me, in two days, and I wrote about it. I watched the other four to the last ball. Then the series ended, an English summer came and went, and I could not name you one innings. Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write, and the universe, with its usual disregard for my sleep, took the job. My resistance lasted about one session.

Chapter Two: Two Rooms

Same city. Same Saturday night

In the first room, a performer who has done this show 200 times walks onto a stage built for it. The lighting is rehearsed. The song you came for arrives second, exactly where it was promised. The audience paid for that, and it is delivered to the minute. Nobody leaves disappointed and nobody leaves changed. This is entertainment, and I have nothing against it. Its virtue is that it keeps its word.

In the second room, a band walks out with sketches and no plan. In the spring of 1959 Miles Davis brought his musicians into a studio with little more than a handful of scales and melodic outlines, and what they made became the best-selling jazz record of all time. It could have been a mess. The patron in that room knows it could have been a mess, because he has sat through the nights when it was. He pays for the chance to find out.

The two audiences differ in more than taste. The first judges the evening against a promise. The second judges himself against the evening: was I paying enough attention to be there when it happened? Entertainment asks whether you enjoyed it. Art asks whether you were awake.

Test cricket is the second room, stretched to five days.

Part Two: The Match

Chapter Three: Tuesday

Newlands, day one

The series stands at one all. Australia won in Durban by 214, on Matt Renshaw’s 190. South Africa won in Gqeberha by an innings and 31 runs, on Temba Bavuma’s 179. Cape Town decides it.

Pat Cummins wins the toss and chooses to field, citing moisture in the pitch. A captain has made that choice at Newlands only 12 times since 1889. The moisture turns out to be a rumour. By lunch Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram have South Africa at 140 without loss.

Ackerman is playing his second Test. He makes 95 off 94 balls, with twelve fours and two sixes, four of the fours in a row off Mitchell Starc. Then, five runs short of a hundred, he walks down the pitch to Nathan Lyon, who has waited 15 years for that look on a batter’s face. Stumped. Afterward Ackerman says he lives by the sword and dies by it, and that he left a hundred out there. He does not pretend to be happy about it.

Then Starc.

There is a kind of bowler around whom an afternoon changes ownership. Wasim Akram is one. Shane Warne was another. The scoreboard was never the evidence. The evidence was the batter, who knew first. On Tuesday evening Starc joins them. He has Bedingham caught on 50 and, two balls later, Wiaan Mulder, caught behind for a duck. He takes Rickelton and Jansen in a single over with the new ball, then Coetzee and Rabada. South Africa fall from 203 for 1 to 329 all out. Starc finishes with six for 72, his 20th five-wicket haul, and he is not done.

Mulder walks off with a zero beside his name. Keep that number.

In the last half hour of the day Starc is bowling himself off his feet, and at the start of his 22nd over he reaches down for his right calf and runs in anyway.

Chapter Four: Wednesday

Day two

Simon Harmer has Travis Head chopping on for 41. Then Labuschagne, going back to a ball that wanted him forward, edges it to slip, where Aiden Markram takes the catch. Five balls. No runs. He arrived at Newlands needing a score to keep his place, and Australia are 58 for 2.

Tuesday, Mulder: nought. Wednesday, Labuschagne: nought. The match sets them side by side and says nothing.

I am travelling, and the Test starts at an hour that my body, wherever it thinks it is, cannot place. By the second night I have moved two meetings. By the fourth I have moved the rest. I, who could not spare 10 minutes for cricket since the Ashes, now discover that I have five days.

Chapter Five: Friday

Day four

Thursday belongs to Australia. Josh Inglis makes 102 off 135 balls and, with Alex Carey, who makes 80, adds 185. Australia lead by 100. By the close South Africa are four down and 40 ahead, a lead you could carry in one hand.

Friday belongs to two men who have known each other since school. Ryan Rickelton already owns a Test double century and is still the quieter name in a batting order that includes Aiden Markram and Temba Bavuma. Mulder walked off on Tuesday with a zero.

Their plan is a lesson in humility. Rickelton has decided to take a few on the body rather than play the short ball, and he does. He spends 37 balls in the 90s. On 92, Starc bangs one in short, Rickelton shoulders arms, and it thuds into his ribs. He lifts his shirt to show Travis Head, at short leg, the bruise coming up, for confirmation or approval. Head, by all accounts, offers both.

Rickelton reaches his hundred after tea and finishes on 101 off 219 balls. Then Mulder reverse-sweeps, Josh Inglis dives at backward point to cut it off, and Rickelton is run out, the stumps broken by Labuschagne. The stand is worth 154.

It would be easier to say that Mulder rescued South Africa. What he does is odder. He rescues himself, and South Africa happens to be standing next to him. He makes 115 off 221 balls, and on the stroke of stumps he clubs Cummins to deep midwicket, where Mitchell Starc, who has done everything else on this ground for three days, takes the catch. South Africa have 387. Australia need 288.

Wiaan Mulder. Tuesday: 0. Friday: 115.

The same 387 would have been a decent total on Tuesday. On Friday, on a pitch that has begun to come apart, from a side that was four down the night before, it is a verdict.

Nothing else in sport asks you to be brave slowly, and then makes you wait through the night to learn whether it counted.

Chapter Six: Saturday Morning

Day five

Kagiso Rabada has the new ball. Travis Head takes a single off the second delivery. The third is down the leg side, Matt Renshaw, the hero of Durban, is strangled, and Rickelton takes the catch behind the stumps. A golden duck. Labuschagne gets up off his haunches and walks out.

Labuschagne, playing no shot, is hit on the back pad in front of the stumps. Richard Kettleborough raises his finger. Labuschagne reviews. The replay shows the ball clipping the off bail, which makes it umpire’s call, and the original decision stands. Out for four. 5-2.

Umpire’s call is a rule written for doubt. If the ball is only clipping the stump, the umpire’s original decision stands, whatever it was. Had Kettleborough shaken his head, the very same replay would have left Labuschagne standing where he was.

I have thought about the innings that follows that headshake more than I have thought about most of the ones that were played. It starts the way his best always have, quietly: a leave, a leave, a punch through cover that sounds like a door closing on a bad year.

This is what faith costs in Test cricket, and what luck pays out. Everything Labuschagne has done since he was a boy, the dawn nets, the leaves, the belief, is weighed in the end against a sliver of bail and one man’s reading of it.

Luck is not the opposite of skill in this game. It is the second signature on the contract. A batter can prepare for everything except the sliver, and the sliver is where Test cricket keeps its mystery.

I wrote once about Virat Kohli and the fifth stump, that line outside off where a ball extends an invitation and a great batter accepts it against his own training.

Kohli was beaten by the ball he should have left. Labuschagne was beaten by the ball he left. The craft is the same and so is the verdict: the sport does not care how well you prepared. I support South Africa. I have rarely been so sorry to see them succeed.

By the end of the day Nathan Lyon, at number 10, will have made 33 not out, the top score of the innings, 29 more than a man who was once the best batter in the world.

Labuschagne has the application, the talent, the faith and the hours. All of it is still there. And one morning, for no reason anyone can name, it leaves, the way a word does when you say it too many times and it becomes a sound. He may have played his last Test for Australia in that over. I hope not.

Marnus Labuschagne. Wednesday: 0. Saturday: 4.

Head scores the way a vending machine dispenses: promptly, correctly, and without looking at you. He hits a few boundaries, then edges Rabada to Marco Jansen at gully. 14. It is Rabada’s 350th Test wicket, reached in 13,808 balls, faster than any bowler in history and 911 balls quicker than Dale Steyn. I am alarmed by how much I enjoy it.

Simon Harmer comes on in the 12th over, and the morning comes apart. Inglis is run out for four after Cameron Green sets off for a run that was never on, and Ackerman, who left a hundred on the field on Tuesday, takes a wicket back from silly point.

Alex Carey reverse-sweeps and top-edges to Jansen. Cooper Connolly is caught behind for nought. Starc, promoted to number eight to deal with the footmarks, survives 25 balls without scoring and is caught at bat-pad off the last ball before lunch, the longest duck of his Test career. At lunch Australia are 60 for 7. Harmer has 3-5 from eight overs.

Chapter Seven: Saturday Afternoon

Day five, after lunch.

After lunch the match stops moving, and it becomes the best thing in it. Australia score two runs in an hour. There is a stretch of 78 balls without a run. Green is sheltered from Harmer’s off breaks, and Cummins, who has come out beside him with a plan to bat time instead of runs, defends everything that comes.

Six fielders crouch around the bat. It is a standoff in which the only weapon anyone holds is patience. When the first run finally comes, the Newlands crowd cheers it, ironically and at length. Then Harmer changes ends, drags one through Green’s gate, and Green is bowled for 27. 62-8.

And then two men who have no business being dangerous become dangerous. Cummins faces 90 balls and scores 11 runs, and I have never been prouder of a ratio. Nathan Lyon, who bowled 44 overs in South Africa’s second innings, bats as though that were a warm-up. They add 45. The result was settled hours ago. They know it, the crowd knows it, and everyone awake across the world knows it. They stay anyway.

This is the strange, magnificent design of the thing. A Test match asks the athlete to bring his best courage and his best stamina not for an hour but for five days. Then, on the fifth afternoon, when the specialists have failed, it hands the match to the people who were hired to do something else.

A fast bowler walks out and decides to become a wall. A spinner decides to become a clock. Nothing they do will change the result, and that is exactly why it matters. A win is a fact. This is a gift.

When a man spends 90 balls on something that cannot be won, the scoreboard stops being the point, and the rest of us find out what valour looks like once the reward has been taken away.

Just before tea Harmer traps Cummins lbw. Cummins reviews. The ball is clipping the off bail, and the umpire’s call stands. It is the second time that day those words have decided a man’s fate, and both times the call goes South Africa’s way.

Harmer finishes with 6 for 16 from 21.1 overs, 14 of them maidens, and 10 wickets in the match, the first time he has done that in a Test. He is 37. He bowled through a torn nail on Thursday. He spent years with Essex in English county cricket, was recalled, and on a Saturday in Cape Town takes apart the top-ranked Test side in the world.

Part Three: The Vigil

Chapter Eight: Everyone Awake

Some hours later.

A machine can give you the result of this Test in one line. It will be correct, and it will take four seconds. Australia 111, South Africa by 176, the series 2-1.

It cannot tell you what it was like to be awake for it.

We are living through a strange subtraction. Answers arrive before the questions are finished. Summaries sit above the thing they summarise. Almost everything that once cost an afternoon now costs a tap, and the cost was never the enemy.

The cost was where the meaning was kept. A letter mattered because it took a week. A song mattered because you had to wait for the radio to play it. Take away the wait and you take away the room where the feeling lived.

Test cricket is the last large public thing built so that nothing can be skipped. You cannot fast-forward the 90th ball. You cannot be told how it felt. The only way to know is to stay, and staying is the whole price of admission, paid in the oldest currency we have: hours, spent in company.

Somewhere in that fifth afternoon, in a time zone that had no business being awake, a stranger was watching Cummins defend a ball for a reason no efficiency expert would accept. Most of us had no stake in the result. We were there because the sport asks a very human question, which is whether you will stay.

That is human-centred design. The game is built to the scale of a person. It takes five days because a person needs five days to become who he will be on the fifth. It lets a man fail in public and return in the second innings.

It makes 10 team-mates watch each member be afraid, one at a time, and know exactly what it costs. And in an age that can produce the likeness of almost anything, it offers the one thing that cannot be produced: a reason to stay up with strangers for something that may not end well, and to be glad you did.

Chapter Nine: Thank You

16 months earlier, and also now.

In June 2025 I sat at Lord’s through Rabada’s third-innings spell of the World Test Championship final and watched Bavuma lift the mace. It was South Africa’s first global title in 27 years, and it was the day and the occasion that moved me most that year.

That same summer I wrote about a five-Test series and called the piece Five Shades of Flat. Now the same South Africans, under Bavuma, who lost the first Test of this series and won the next two, are the number one Test side in the world for the first time since January 2016.

Thank you Test Cricket..

Thank you For lunch, to begin with, which stops a Test match at its most dangerous moment so that twenty-two men can have a civilized meal.

For tea, the second truce of the day.

For the maiden over, the only unit of achievement in sport defined by nothing happening.

For the duck, a zero named after a bird, so that even the worst day a batter can have arrives with a little feathered mercy.

For a game in which a man can score eleven in ninety balls and be remembered as a hero, and another can score four in three balls and be mourned.

For umpire’s call, in which a machine admits it is not sure.

For the nightwatchman, the bad light, the follow-on, the draw that feels like a victory and the victory that feels like a funeral.

We could not have invented you. No committee would have approved you. You take five days to say what other sports say in two hours, and you say it better, because you leave room for people to be wrong in public and the time for them to come back.

I closed the laptop. The room was quiet, and the quiet was full, the way a house is after the guests have gone. Whether Marnus Labuschagne walks out again for Australia is the one thing this match left unanswered. Test cricket will answer in its own time. I intend to be awake when it does.

Yours, awake.. I suspect he is too.

cleaned_blocks.text: Newlands, Cape Town. Saturday morning, before the first ball.

Marnus Labuschagne crouches on his haunches at the edge of the outfield, waiting to bat. Australia need 288 to win the Test and the series. In the first innings he made a five-ball duck. He has scored 11 Test hundreds, and the last came at Old Trafford in July 2023. For a stretch he was the best batter in the world.
He stands, walks to the middle, and takes guard. He will face three balls. I have not stopped thinking about them.
Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write…
Chapter One: Moved
Some months earlier

I write about this game only when it moves me. Good cricket does not count. Good cricket arrives every week and asks nothing of you. Being moved is rarer: a stranger does something you did not know a person could do, in a country you may never see, at an hour when you should be asleep, and for a few minutes you stop being an audience and become a witness. The first Test of the Ashes did that to me, in two days, and I wrote about it. I watched the other four to the last ball. Then the series ended, an English summer came and went, and I could not name you one innings. Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write, and the universe, with its usual disregard for my sleep, took the job. My resistance lasted about one session.
Chapter Two: Two Rooms
Same city. Same Saturday night

In the first room, a performer who has done this show 200 times walks onto a stage built for it. The lighting is rehearsed. The song you came for arrives second, exactly where it was promised. The audience paid for that, and it is delivered to the minute. Nobody leaves disappointed and nobody leaves changed. This is entertainment, and I have nothing against it. Its virtue is that it keeps its word.

In the second room, a band walks out with sketches and no plan. In the spring of 1959 Miles Davis brought his musicians into a studio with little more than a handful of scales and melodic outlines, and what they made became the best-selling jazz record of all time. It could have been a mess. The patron in that room knows it could have been a mess, because he has sat through the nights when it was. He pays for the chance to find out.

The two audiences differ in more than taste. The first judges the evening against a promise. The second judges himself against the evening: was I paying enough attention to be there when it happened? Entertainment asks whether you enjoyed it. Art asks whether you were awake.
Test cricket is the second room, stretched to five days.
Chapter Three: Tuesday
Newlands, day one
The series stands at one all. Australia won in Durban by 214, on Matt Renshaw’s 190. South Africa won in Gqeberha by an innings and 31 runs, on Temba Bavuma’s 179. Cape Town decides it.

Pat Cummins wins the toss and chooses to field, citing moisture in the pitch. A captain has made that choice at Newlands only 12 times since 1889. The moisture turns out to be a rumour. By lunch Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram have South Africa at 140 without loss.

Ackerman is playing his second Test. He makes 95 off 94 balls, with twelve fours and two sixes, four of the fours in a row off Mitchell Starc. Then, five runs short of a hundred, he walks down the pitch to Nathan Lyon, who has waited 15 years for that look on a batter’s face. Stumped. Afterward Ackerman says he lives by the sword and dies by it, and that he left a hundred out there. He does not pretend to be happy about it.
Then Starc.

There is a kind of bowler around whom an afternoon changes ownership. Wasim Akram is one. Shane Warne was another. The scoreboard was never the evidence. The evidence was the batter, who knew first. On Tuesday evening Starc joins them. He has Bedingham caught on 50 and, two balls later, Wiaan Mulder, caught behind for a duck. He takes Rickelton and Jansen in a single over with the new ball, then Coetzee and Rabada. South Africa fall from 203 for 1 to 329 all out. Starc finishes with six for 72, his 20th five-wicket haul, and he is not done.
Mulder walks off with a zero beside his name. Keep that number.
In the last half hour of the day Starc is bowling himself off his feet, and at the start of his 22nd over he reaches down for his right calf and runs in anyway.
Chapter Four: Wednesday
Day two

Simon Harmer has Travis Head chopping on for 41. Then Labuschagne, going back to a ball that wanted him forward, edges it to slip, where Aiden Markram takes the catch. Five balls. No runs. He arrived at Newlands needing a score to keep his place, and Australia are 58 for 2.
Tuesday, Mulder: nought. Wednesday, Labuschagne: nought. The match sets them side by side and says nothing.

I am travelling, and the Test starts at an hour that my body, wherever it thinks it is, cannot place. By the second night I have moved two meetings. By the fourth I have moved the rest. I, who could not spare 10 minutes for cricket since the Ashes, now discover that I have five days.
Chapter Five: Friday
Day four

Thursday belongs to Australia. Josh Inglis makes 102 off 135 balls and, with Alex Carey, who makes 80, adds 185. Australia lead by 100. By the close South Africa are four down and 40 ahead, a lead you could carry in one hand.

Head, by all accounts, offers both.

South Africa have 387. Australia need 288.
Wiaan Mulder. Tuesday: 0. Friday: 115.
The same 387 would have been a decent total on Tuesday. On Friday, on a pitch that has begun to come apart, from a side that was four down the night before, it is a verdict.

Day five

David Warner had predicted that the day would end with Labuschagne a 100 not out and Australia winning with seven wickets down.

The first ball Marnus faces runs off the leading edge, past gully, for four. Two balls later Rabada bowls one that nips back. Labuschagne, playing no shot, is hit on the back pad in front of the stumps. Richard Kettleborough raises his finger. Labuschagne reviews. The replay shows the ball clipping the off bail, which makes it umpire’s call, and the original decision stands. Out for four. 5-2.

Umpire’s call is a rule written for doubt. If the ball is only clipping the stump, the umpire’s original decision stands, whatever it was. Had Kettleborough shaken his head, the very same replay would have left Labuschagne standing where he was.

I have thought about the innings that follows that headshake more than I have thought about most of the ones that were played. It starts the way his best always have, quietly: a leave, a leave, a punch through cover that sounds like a door closing on a bad year.

And one morning, for no reason anyone can name, it leaves, the way a word does when you say it too many times and it becomes a sound. He may have played his last Test for Australia in that over. I hope not.
Marnus Labuschagne. Wednesday: 0. Saturday: 4.

At lunch Australia are 60 for 7. Harmer has 3-5 from eight overs.

Day five, after lunch.

Green is sheltered from Harmer’s off breaks, and Cummins, who has come out beside him with a plan to bat time instead of runs, defends everything that comes.

headline: Kuwait lifts oil output to highest since start of Iran war, source says
description: Kuwait raised its crude oil production to 2.1 million barrels per day in October, the highest level since the...
article_text:
Kuwait raised its crude oil production to 2.1 million barrels per day in October, the highest level since the outbreak of the Iran war and a rise of over 300,000 bpd from September, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.

The increase came despite a record number of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to signs that Gulf oil producers are maintaining or increasing output as they adapt to the disruption risks.

The person asked not to be named because they were not authorised to speak publicly about Kuwaiti production.
