headline: China calls for Middle East dialogue in talks with Iran, Saudi Arabia, Oman
description: The meetings come days after US President Donald Trump issued a fresh war threat more than eight months into the conflict.
author: AFP
article_text:
China stepped up diplomatic efforts on Monday to resolve the Middle East crisis, urging a return to the negotiating table in back-to-back meetings with Iranian, Omani and Saudi officials in Beijing.

The meetings come days after United States President Donald Trump issued a fresh war threat more than eight months into the conflict, which was triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Iran and has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries.

Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security”, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a Chinese statement.

Wang later called for dialogue to end the conflict “while safeguarding regional energy security and the safety of shipping lanes”, as he met with Saudi National Security Adviser Musaad bin Mohammad al-Aiban.

China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought a detente in the months-long conflict that has disrupted global shipping.

Trump said on Saturday that the United States had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, with Tehran warning of reprisals if attacked.

“All parties should… in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict,” Wang told Bagheri Kani, according to the statement.

China’s foreign ministry had not previously announced the visit by Bagheri Kani to Beijing.

President Xi Jinping also met Oman’s sultan for talks in Beijing on Monday — the first visit to China by the Gulf nation’s head of state since diplomatic ties were established.

Xi told Haitham bin Tariq that China was ready to “contribute to peace, stability and prosperity in the region”.

The Chinese leader said that the Middle East should not become a “wrestling ground for major-country rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”, state news agency Xinhua reported.

Later this month, Beijing will send its Middle East envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia as part of “shuttle diplomacy visits… aimed at promoting peace talks (and) easing tensions”, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson told a news briefing.

headline: Fridge cyberattack hits supermarkets across Europe
description: Stores in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Luxembourg and Sweden witness temperatures in their cold cases soar, raising concerns of spoiled food and food security.
author: AFP
article_text:
Grocery stores in at least five European countries saw temperatures in their cold cases soar on Monday, with several confirming they had been hit by a cyberattack similar to one three weeks ago in France.

Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Luxembourg and Sweden were among those affected in the latest hacker attack.

Major French retailers said on Oct 12 that hundreds of store refrigeration systems were hit by a cyberattack, which forced them to throw out spoiled food and raised concerns about food security.

No one has claimed responsibility for either attack.

Carrefour Belgium on Monday reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 stores.

“It’s a cyberattack; there is no other reason,” said spokesman Mich Vergauwen.

An Ikea Belgium spokeswoman likewise said a cyberattack hit its store in Mons, southwestern Belgium, causing the temperature of freezers to rise suddenly in the early hours of Monday.

Chains Delhaize, Colruyt and Intermarche also experienced technical problems affecting their fridges in Belgium, while Delhaize reported that four of its stores in Luxembourg were also affected.

Belgian industrial refrigeration group Sabcobel said it had begun securing its installations after the Oct 12 attack in France, but around 10 per cent were still not fixed, and some were in the shops affected on Monday.

“If Sabcobel hadn’t started this operation … the impact would have been much more important,” chief executive Stephan Moelans told AFP.

In Sweden, chain Coop confirmed six of its around 800 stores had been hit by a cyberattack early Monday.

“We can confirm that it is a cyber incident. The problem has now been resolved, and the fridges and freezers are working as normal,” spokesman Carlos Cancino told AFP.

He said Coop did not know who was behind the attack, but noted that the six affected stores had been connected to a 4G mobile network, not the updated 5G system, which made them “more exposed” to hackers.

‘Vulnerabilities’

Swedish chain Ica also said “a limited number” of its stores experienced refrigeration problems, but the group could not confirm a cyberattack was the cause.

According to Ica spokesperson Helena Johansson, the affected stores were all connected to an external refrigeration control system provided by Danish manufacturer Danfoss — the same supplier targeted in the Oct 12 cyberattack on French retailers.

She referred all queries to Danfoss.

It has not responded to AFP’s request for a comment.

One Ica store located in Sjobo, in southern Sweden, posted on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had “been hacked and they set the temperature at 50 degrees” Celsius.

In Finland, irregular temperatures had also been detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group.

“We are currently investigating the cause, and interference via the network has not yet been ruled out,” Petri Kayhko, head of Kesko’s corporate security, told AFP.

Roni Kokkola, an information security specialist at the National Cyber Security Centre at Finland’s Transport and Communications Agency Traficom, would not rule out cyber interference “as far as Finland is concerned”.

“We’ve seen this in Europe in the past few months, so it spreading beyond France to other countries has been expected,” he told AFP.

“Nowadays it’s very typical that all kinds of vulnerabilities are being exploited ever more actively and rapidly.”

In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50°C, public broadcaster ERR reported.

The units were older models delivered by Danfoss, similar to the ones targeted in the France attack, Jann Mutso, director of Kitman Coldtech, a manufacturer and distributor of advanced refrigeration systems, told ERR.

“The handwriting is the same, but I can’t say more,” Mutso said.

Following the attack in France, Danfoss told AFP that most of the affected equipment were “legacy” products which “no longer receive software or security updates”.

EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said at the time that “food security requires more attention at all levels”.

The “exploitation of food” was now a “reality”, he added.

The units were older models delivered by Danfoss, similar to the ones targeted in the France attack, Jann Mutso, director of Kitman Coldtech, a manufacturer and distributor of advanced refrigeration systems, told ERR.
“The handwriting is the same, but I can’t say more,” Mutso said.
Following the attack in France, Danfoss told AFP that most of the affected equipment were “legacy” products which “no longer receive software or security updates”.
EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said at the time that “food security requires more attention at all levels”.
The “exploitation of food” was now a “reality”, he added.

headline: Iran VP says indirect exchanges with US point to recognition of Tehran's 'victory'
description: Iran’s vice president says exchanges with the United States via mediators indicate Washington’s recognition of...
article_text:
Iran’s vice president says exchanges with the United States via mediators indicate Washington’s recognition of Tehran’s “victory” in the Middle East war, AFP reports.

“Our enemy failed to achieve any of its objectives in the last two wars. Even today, although the United States, driven by its own goals and concerns regarding domestic public opinion, is engaging in various manoeuvres, the messages conveyed to Iran through intermediaries point to an acknowledgement of our victory,” Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref is quoted as saying by the IRNA state news agency.

headline: Adrian Hamilton-Manns appointed new PIA chief executive officer
description: PIA says the appointment “marks a pivotal chapter” in the airline’s ongoing transformation.
author: News Desk
article_text:
The board of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) on Monday announced the appointment of Adrian Hamilton-Manns as its chief executive officer (CEO).

In a press release, PIA said Hamilton-Manns “brings a wealth of leadership and strategic experience within the global aviation sector”, adding that his appointment “marks a pivotal chapter” in the airline’s ongoing transformation.

It said that he had managed three airlines as CEO and was considered a “world expert” in transforming and reviving airlines, with over 30 years of experience.

“As Hamilton-Manns assumes the role of CEO, the consortium and the entire management board extend their deepest gratitude to the outgoing CEO, Air Vice Marshal (AVM) Amir Hayat, for his outstanding service and dedication to this vital national role,” the statement said.

It added that over his four-and-a-half-year tenure, Hayat’s leadership was “instrumental in navigating the airline through significant industry challenges”.

“His relentless efforts were central to initiating comprehensive structural reforms, optimising operational efficiencies and successfully preparing the airline for its highly anticipated privatisation phase,” it said.

“The foundation he has laid will be critical to the carrier’s future commercial viability and success,” it added.

The statement said that with Hamilton-Manns at the helm, PIA was confident that his extensive industry expertise would accelerate strategic objectives, elevate service standards and drive sustainable profitability in this new era.

According to Forbes Middle East, Hamilton-Manns was previously the CEO of Oman’s SalamAir and Kazakhstan-based FlyArystan. He also held roles at South African Airways and Virgin Australia.

The national flag carrier was privatised in December last year through an auction. A consortium led by Arif Habib Corporation Limited had won the auction for 75 per cent shares of PIA in December last year, making a winning bid of Rs135 billion.

The Arif Habib-led consortium, which took charge in June this year, had vowed to transform the loss-making airline through operational restructuring, fleet expansion, and improved customer service.

On Sunday, the carrier’s first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, acquired on lease last month, arrived in Islamabad from London as flight PK786. A PIA spokesperson said that the carrier was the first Pakistani airline to have added a Boeing 787-9 to its fleet.

headline: Forget my phone, can hackers access my fridge?
description: If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked.
author: Reuters
article_text:
Ahold Delhaize said on Monday that an “IT incident” had hit fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg.

In October, the retailer reported an earlier cybersecurity incident to the Dutch police, coinciding with a cyberattack in France that caused refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of stores to heat up to 50°Celsius overnight, sparking fires and spoiling food.

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

Can hackers really get into my fridge?

In theory, yes. If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked.

In 2015, researchers demonstrated at a Las Vegas hacking conference how a Samsung smart refrigerator could be compromised, allowing them to intercept some of the internet traffic passing through the device.

In many cases, attackers are more interested in stealing data, disrupting services or using connected devices as a way into a larger network.

What household devices could be hacked?

The most common targets are devices connected to the internet and controlled remotely. These include security cameras, video doorbells, alarm systems, smart locks, thermostats and central heating systems.

Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens and washing machines can also be vulnerable if they are connected to the wider internet. Even some toothbrushes are now internet-connected.

Routers, not appliances, account for more than three-quarters of all attacks on connected devices, according to security-industry data.

The number of such devices has grown rapidly as manufacturers have added internet connectivity to products that were once entirely mechanical.

What could a hacker actually do?

Once inside a device, a hacker can generally do one of two things: gather information or take control of the device.

A camera can show the inside of a home, a device with a microphone can pick up sound, and a compromised router can expose everything that travels through the network.

Hackers who take control of a device can switch it on or off, change settings or lock users out of their accounts. A compromised thermostat could affect heating, while a hacked freezer or refrigerator could disrupt temperature controls.

In more serious cases, attackers may use poorly secured devices to gain access to other systems on the same network or to steal personal information linked to online accounts.

Could hackers take over my car, electricity or water supply?

Cybersecurity researchers have repeatedly demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles.

In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes.

Nearly a decade later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only a licence plate number. The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited in real-world attacks.

Modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems.

Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that are not present in consumer devices.

That does not mean they are immune from cyberattacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi-Fi network.

How can people protect their devices?

Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available, and regularly installing software updates.

Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so.

The simplest rule is often the most effective: the fewer connected devices you have, the fewer potential entry points exist for attackers.

Ahold Delhaize said on Monday that an “IT incident” had hit fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg.

In October, the retailer reported an earlier cybersecurity incident to the Dutch police, coinciding with a cyberattack in France that caused refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of stores to heat up to 50°Celsius overnight, sparking fires and spoiling food.

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

Can hackers really get into my fridge?

In theory, yes. If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked.

In 2015, researchers demonstrated at a Las Vegas hacking conference how a Samsung smart refrigerator could be compromised, allowing them to intercept some of the internet traffic passing through the device.

In many cases, attackers are more interested in stealing data, disrupting services or using connected devices as a way into a larger network.

What household devices could be hacked?

The most common targets are devices connected to the internet and controlled remotely. These include security cameras, video doorbells, alarm systems, smart locks, thermostats and central heating systems.

Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens and washing machines can also be vulnerable if they are connected to the wider internet. Even some toothbrushes are now internet-connected.

Routers, not appliances, account for more than three-quarters of all attacks on connected devices, according to security-industry data.

The number of such devices has grown rapidly as manufacturers have added internet connectivity to products that were once entirely mechanical.

What could a hacker actually do?

Once inside a device, a hacker can generally do one of two things: gather information or take control of the device.

A camera can show the inside of a home, a device with a microphone can pick up sound, and a compromised router can expose everything that travels through the network.

Hackers who take control of a device can switch it on or off, change settings or lock users out of their accounts. A compromised thermostat could affect heating, while a hacked freezer or refrigerator could disrupt temperature controls.

In more serious cases, attackers may use poorly secured devices to gain access to other systems on the same network or to steal personal information linked to online accounts.

Could hackers take over my car, electricity or water supply?

Cybersecurity researchers have repeatedly demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles.

In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes.

Nearly a decade later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only a licence plate number. The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited in real-world attacks.

Modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems.

Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that are not present in consumer devices.

That does not mean they are immune from cyberattacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi-Fi network.

How can people protect their devices?

Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available, and regularly installing software updates.

Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so.

The simplest rule is often the most effective: the fewer connected devices you have, the fewer potential entry points exist for attackers.

headline: Houthis claim attacks on Jizan, Dammam airports in Saudi Arabia

article_text:
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree claims that over the past 48 hours, the group targeted airports in Dammam and Jizan, causing damage to military equipment and disrupting air traffic.

He claims the group targeted Dammam Airport in two phases using two drones, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport.

“Meanwhile, the early warning radar in Jizan was targeted with a drone, achieving a direct hit. Additionally, a military transport aircraft at Jizan Airport was targeted,” Saree adds.

headline: Pakistan, China discuss regional and global developments in high-level meetings
description: Liu Haixing of China's ruling party CPC, who is visiting Pakistan, calls on PM Shehbaz, DPM Dar and CDF Munir.
author: News Desk
article_text:
Pakistan and China on Monday discussed regional and global developments as a visiting official of Beijing’s ruling party met with the country’s top leadership.

Liu Haixing, minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China’s Central Committee (IDCPC), arrived in Islamabad on a three-day visit last night. The department is in charge of the CPC’s external relations.

During his meeting with Haixing and his delegation, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reaffirmed that Pakistan and China enjoyed an “ironclad, time-tested and all-weather strategic cooperative partnership”, the premier’s office (PMO) said.

“Both sides exchanged views on regional and international developments and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining close coordination and cooperation at bilateral and multilateral forums,” the PMO statement read.

The prime minister underscored that Pakistan-China friendship was anchored in mutual trust, mutual respect and deep-rooted bonds between the people of both countries.

Reaffirming Pakistan’s commitment to working closely with China, PM Shehbaz commended the “shared focus on advancing cooperation in trade, investment, connectivity, infrastructure development, IT and agriculture modernisation”.

He stressed the importance of sustained political engagement and party-to-party exchanges in further strengthening the bilateral relations.

He also appreciated the important role played by the IDCPC in fostering institutional linkages and promoting cooperation between the political leadership of the two countries.

On his part, Haixing “appreciated the ongoing momentum in high-level and party-to-party exchanges, aimed at further bolstering the iron-clad friendship between the two countries”, PMO said.

He conveyed the greetings of the Chinese leadership and reaffirmed China’s commitment to further deepening its longstanding friendship with Pakistan, the statement added.

PM Shehbaz also hosted a banquet in honour of the visiting dignitary and the accompanying Chinese delegation.

Meeting with CDF Munir

In a separate meeting, Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir discussed “evolving regional and international security dynamics and bilateral relations” with Haixing, the military’s media wing said.

The visiting CPC official called on CDF Munir at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, according to a statement by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

Besides discussing matters of mutual interest, both sides “expressed their shared resolve to further strengthen the all-weather strategic cooperative partnership between Pakistan and China”, ISPR said.

CDF Munir highlighted the “historic and time-tested bond between the two countries and emphasised the importance of sustained high-level engagement, stronger institutional linkages and expanded cooperation across areas of mutual interest”.

China’s Haixing appreciated Pakistan’s contributions to regional peace and stability and expressed confidence in further advancing the longstanding strategic partnership between the two countries, according to the statement.

Islamabad, Beijing agree to maintain close coordination

Separately, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also held a bilateral meeting with the IDCPC minister in Islamabad.

The Chinese dignitary conveyed greetings from FM Wang Yi, which DPM Dar “warmly reciprocated”, according to the Foreign Office (FO).

On his part, Dar also conveyed “warm greetings” to President Xi Jinping on behalf of Pakistan’s leadership.

He also reaffirmed Islamabad’s “continued commitment to further strengthening the all-weather strategic cooperative partnership” with Beijing.

“The two sides discussed ways to enhance cultural ties and people-to-people exchanges,” FO added.

Both leaders, according to FO, expressed their resolve to maintain close coordination and carry forward the “positive momentum” in bilateral relations.

Haixing’s visit is “part of the ongoing high-level exchanges between Pakistan and China, reflecting the longstanding friendship and all-weather strategic cooperative partnership between the two countries”, FO had said earlier.

Recently, Pakistan and China signed an agreement to operationalise a green channel at the Sost-Khunjerab border for agricultural and allied products to facilitate bilateral trade. Khunjerab Pass connects Gilgit-Baltistan with China’s Xinjiang region and is the highest paved international border at 15,500 feet above sea level.

Also last week, the two countries launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor (CPIC), which will be based on four pillars — media, business and enterprises, think tanks, and culture/tourism.

Pakistan and China share a longstanding strategic partnership rooted in mutual trust, economic cooperation and regional connectivity.

Over the decades, ties have expanded across various sectors — including trade, energy, defence, infrastructure and space — with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) symbolising a shared vision for development.

headline: Fuel prices
Oil prices plunge on US-Iran detente hopes ahead of midterms
description: Oil prices have sunk around seven per cent, on the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals...
article_text:
Oil prices have sunk around seven per cent, on the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington are renewing dialogue boost hopes of ending the war, AFP reports.

Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks. That was the highest-level move from the administration of US President Donald Trump in months.

“We believe the (Trump) signals may be tactical ahead of tomorrow’s US midterm elections,” noted Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at Global Risk Management. “Meanwhile, attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz continue (and) we maintain our higher-for-longer outlook for energy prices.”

Nevertheless, share prices of energy majors have dropped, while many other sectors are boosted by the cooling fuel costs.

Traders are also focused on Tuesday’s midterms, with Democrats expecting to win at least partial control of Congress that would impose political constraints on Trump for the first time in two years.

headline: PTI lawyer Salman Safdar says he met Imran, Bushra Bibi at Adiala jail
description: Counsel says meeting lasted 40 minutes and was “insufficient to cover all cases [and] legal matters”.
author: News Desk, Ikram Junaidi
article_text:
PTI lawyer Barrister Salman Safdar on Monday said he met with party founder Imran Khan and his spouse, Bushra Bibi, at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail, where they are both incarcerated.

Imran has been in prison since Aug 5, 2023, while his wife was arrested on Jan 17, 2025 in a separate case in which the couple were sentenced.

The IHC has allowed Imran twice-a-week meetings — on Tuesdays and Thursdays — with his family, lawyers and other associates. Despite multiple court directives, Imran’s meetings with his family and party leaders have been largely restricted in recent months.

In a post on X on Monday, Safdar said the meeting was his first with Imran after seven months and with Bushra in 11 months.

The last time he met Imran, the Supreme Court designated him as amicus. However, this time he met Imran Khan as his lawyer.

It lasted 40 minutes and was “insufficient to cover all cases [and] legal matters”, the PTI counsel contended.

“Both briefed me on their health conditions [and living] conditions and gave Fresh instructions for some legal matters and cases,” he wrote on X.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram told Dawn that he spoke to Safdar in detail.

“Salman told me that the meeting was held in connection with a number of applications which have been filed in courts to arrange meetings with Imran Khan,” he said.

“Salman has told me that he reached Adiala Jail at around 4:30pm and the meeting continued for around 40 to 45 minutes. However, he said that it was not sufficient time for the meetings, as there were so many cases which had to be discussed and as the meeting was being held after such a long time.“

Replying to a question, Akram said that no political issues were discussed during the meeting, which he added was also attended by Bushra Bibi. Safdar spoke about the cases and asked about future strategy.

When asked about Imran’s health, Akram replied that although health issues were discussed, the PTI would only speak about the legal cases.

Barrister Safdar’s last publicly reported meeting with Imran was held on April 8 this year, a day after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) directed authorities to arrange the meeting.

His previous meeting on Feb 10 with the former premier was also on the directives of the Supreme Court, where concerns about Imran’s health were raised.

Imran’s eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — came to light in late January. While he has undergone eye procedures at the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), his family demands that he be shifted to a hospital of his choice.

The government and the opposition have been engaged in a blame game, with the latter accusing the former of a lack of transparency on the matter, of not ensuring appropriate treatment for Imran, and of not allowing his personal physicians access to him. The government denies these allegations.

Imran was sent to jail for a three-year term on Aug 5, 2023 for concealing details of Toshakhana gifts. However, he and Bushra are also serving a 14-year sentence in a £190 million corruption case, also known as the Al-Qadir Trust case.

The couple were convicted in another Toshakhana case in December 2025, with 10-year and seven-year terms handed to them. The PTI founder also faces pending trials in terrorism cases related to the May 9, 2023 riots.

Imran’s sisters Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan, along with opposition leaders, have staged frequent sit-ins outside the Adiala jail demanding the PTI founder’s release.

They remain unable to stage more sit-ins since their detention in late September under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, as the PTI geared up for a protest march to Islamabad.

Imran has been in prison since Aug 5, 2023, while his wife was arrested on Jan 17, 2025 in a separate case in which the couple were sentenced.

The IHC has allowed Imran twice-a-week meetings — on Tuesdays and Thursdays — with his family, lawyers and other associates. Despite multiple court directives, Imran’s meetings with his family and party leaders have been largely restricted in recent months.

In a post on X on Monday, Safdar said the meeting was his first with Imran after seven months and with Bushra in 11 months.

The last time he met Imran, the Supreme Court designated him as amicus. However, this time he met Imran Khan as his lawyer.

It lasted 40 minutes and was “insufficient to cover all cases [and] legal matters”, the PTI counsel contended.

“Both briefed me on their health conditions [and living] conditions and gave Fresh instructions for some legal matters and cases,” he wrote on X.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram told Dawn that he spoke to Safdar in detail.

“Salman told me that the meeting was held in connection with a number of applications which have been filed in courts to arrange meetings with Imran Khan,” he said.

“Salman has told me that he reached Adiala Jail at around 4:30pm and the meeting continued for around 40 to 45 minutes. However, he said that it was not sufficient time for the meetings, as there were so many cases which had to be discussed and as the meeting was being held after such a long time.“

Replying to a question, Akram said that no political issues were discussed during the meeting, which he added was also attended by Bushra Bibi. Safdar spoke about the cases and asked about future strategy.

When asked about Imran’s health, Akram replied that although health issues were discussed, the PTI would only speak about the legal cases.

Barrister Safdar’s last publicly reported meeting with Imran was held on April 8 this year, a day after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) directed authorities to arrange the meeting.

His previous meeting on Feb 10 with the former premier was also on the directives of the Supreme Court, where concerns about Imran’s health were raised.

Imran’s eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — came to light in late January. While he has undergone eye procedures at the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), his family demands that he be shifted to a hospital of his choice.

The government and the opposition have been engaged in a blame game, with the latter accusing the former of a lack of transparency on the matter, of not ensuring appropriate treatment for Imran, and of not allowing his personal physicians access to him. The government denies these allegations.

Imran was sent to jail for a three-year term on Aug 5, 2023 for concealing details of Toshakhana gifts. However, he and Bushra are also serving a 14-year sentence in a £190 million corruption case, also known as the Al-Qadir Trust case.

The couple were convicted in another Toshakhana case in December 2025, with 10-year and seven-year terms handed to them. The PTI founder also faces pending trials in terrorism cases related to the May 9, 2023 riots.

Imran’s sisters Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan, along with opposition leaders, have staged frequent sit-ins outside the Adiala jail demanding the PTI founder’s release.

They remain unable to stage more sit-ins since their detention in late September under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, as the PTI geared up for a protest march to Islamabad.

headline: At Kazakhstan forum, Pakistan presents Karachi and Gwadar ports as 'strategic gateways' for Central Asian trade
description: Minister invites investors to explore opportunities in key sectors, including energy, infrastructure, logistics, transportation, manufacturing and trade.
author: Amin Ahmed
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan can serve as an important trade and transit corridor for the landlocked Central Asian countries, providing them with access to international maritime trade routes and global markets, Minister for Board of Investment (BoI) Qaiser Ahmed Sheikh said on Monday.

He made the remarks while addressing the opening session of the Second Tianshan Forum for Central Asian Economic and Quality Investment, being held in Kazakhstan’s Almaty.

The minister termed Pakistan’s three major seaports — Karachi Port, Port Qasim and Gwadar Port — “strategic gateways that could facilitate regional trade, strengthen transportation links and provide alternative routes for the movement of goods”, according to a press release by the BoI.

Sheikh particularly underscored Karachi’s importance as Pakistan’s major industrial and commercial hub, noting that its established industrial base, business infrastructure, financial institutions and port facilities offered significant opportunities for trade, industrial partnerships and foreign investment.

He also highlighted Gwadar’s potential to further strengthen regional connectivity and economic cooperation.

Regional connectivity was “not merely about linking roads, ports and markets, but also about connecting economies, creating investment opportunities, generating employment and building shared prosperity across the region”, he remarked.

The minister invited regional and international investors to explore opportunities in key sectors, including energy, infrastructure, logistics, transportation, manufacturing and trade. He emphasised that improved connectivity and reliable energy supplies were essential for unlocking the region’s economic potential, the BoI statement said.

Highlighting the importance of regional cooperation, the minister acknowledged the contribution of the Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation (Carec) Programme in promoting transport connectivity, facilitating trade and supporting economic integration among participating countries.

He observed that Carec provided a valuable platform for strengthening economic partnerships between Pakistan and Central Asian states, the statement said.

The minister emphasised that Pakistan’s strategic geographical location, youthful population, industrial capacity and seaport infrastructure positioned the country to play an important role in connecting Central Asian economies with international markets.

The Second Tianshan Forum will conclude in Almaty on Tuesday under the theme “Strengthening Resilient Connectivity and Quality Investment in Central Asia”.

According to information provided in its official agenda, the two-day forum is a follow-up to the success of the inaugural Tianshan Forum for Central Asia Economic Cooperation, and is aligned with the new Carec Institute Strategy 2026–2030, as well as the Carec 2030 Strategy Midterm Review Rolling Implementation Action Plan.

“In 2026, the Carec region continues to face a highly uncertain external environment. Rising geopolitical tensions have raised energy and food prices, disrupted transport and logistics, and weakened the reliability of trade corridors,” the agenda said.

At the same time, it added that intra-regional trade remained limited due to similar economic structures, weak production complementarities, and incomplete market opening. Persistent transport and logistics bottlenecks such as uneven infrastructure quality, fragmented asset management, and capacity mismatches kept trade costs high, it added.

“Non-physical barriers, including inconsistent customs procedures, weak digitalisation, non-harmonised standards, and inefficient border operations, further constrain cross-border flows. Meanwhile, digital infrastructure — especially cloud services, data centres, and AI applications — is expanding rapidly and reshaping connectivity and competitiveness,” it said.

It pointed out that Carec countries were progressing unevenly with “large gaps in backbone infrastructure, digital skills, and regulatory coherence”, calling for these gaps to be bridged to “effectively support inclusive growth, resilient connectivity, and regional integration”.

Senior representatives from multilateral development banks, financial institutions, high-level policymakers, business leaders, local governments, and academia across the Carec countries are attending the forum to discuss policy and operational issues in strategic areas such as transport, trade, logistics, energy, and digital connectivity, and promote pragmatic, sustainable investment in the region.

headline: US' greatest military setback lies in collapse of its image of power, Iranian commander says
description: Iranian Army Deputy Chief for Executive Affairs Brigadier General Alireza Sheikh claims that during hostilities, 17...
article_text:
Iranian Army Deputy Chief for Executive Affairs Brigadier General Alireza Sheikh claims that during hostilities, 17 US bases in the region were damaged, 65 per cent of its Patriot interceptor missiles were used, and the Pentagon incurred more than $47 billion in direct costs, state broadcaster Press TV reports.

“America’s greatest military setback goes beyond casualties and material losses; it lies in the collapse of the image of power it spent years and vast resources building,” he is quoted as saying.

“[The] US entered the war to restore its superpower image and show it could impose its will through military force. But the battlefield exposed the limits of that power, showing that military superiority does not guarantee political or strategic success,” he adds.

headline: Yemeni forces say they recaptured territory from Houthis in Taiz province
description: Al Jazeera reports that Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have launched a counterattack against...
article_text:
Al Jazeera reports that Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have launched a counterattack against the Houthis, recapturing more territory in the province of Taiz.

In a post on Facebook, the official page of the Al-Aqroud Front’s Fifth Battalion, 35th Brigade says the Yemeni army, along with Popular Resistance fighters, secured control over the hills of Tabat Wathib and Habil al-Saram during fierce battles with the Houthis.

Coalition forces says dozens of Houthi fighters were killed or injured.

headline: Defence diplomacy
description: Pakistan stands firmly behind its defence commitments to Saudi Arabia, and that credibility is what gave weight to the talks it convened in Tehran.
author: Dr Atia Ali Kazmi
article_text:
When Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Field Marshal Asim Munir and Türkiye’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin sat down in Tehran on Monday with President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, they came as guarantors of the Kingdom’s security, three weeks after activating collective deterrence against those attacking it. Riyadh said the visit was meant to open channels to “prevent the return of military escalation”. That is diplomacy from a position of strength, and the right use of the common defence architecture.

My proposition is simple. Pakistan is a guarantor of Saudi security, and its commitment under the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement is firm.

These pacts are shields for the Kingdom, not swords against any neighbour, and a shield is only as strong as the resolve of those who hold it in their common interests. That resolve gives Pakistan’s diplomacy its weight, and Islamabad should use it to press for a regional non-aggression framework that includes Iran. Deterrence keeps the peace when no one doubts it will be honoured.

Reading between the lines

Consider the texts. In September 2025, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, whose published summary states that “any aggression against either country shall be considered an aggression against both”. Pakistan’s Foreign Office said at the time that it was “defensive in nature and not directed against any third country”. Defensive does not mean tentative: an attack on the Kingdom is an attack on Pakistan and vice versa.

The second instrument, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on August 7, 2026, is more detailed. Article 2 provides that “an externally originating armed attack against any of the ‘Parties’ shall be considered an attack against all”, and the parties “shall determine the scope and nature of the support to be provided following an objective assessment” and act “within the limits of their available resources”. Article 12 preserves obligations under earlier treaties. These are the clauses of a serious alliance: a clear commitment to collective defence, delivered by joint decision.

Neither text names an adversary, and the only invocation shows what the alliance is for, and that it acts. On October 5, after Houthi strikes on the Kingdom, the partners agreed to “activate collective deterrence measures … in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them”. That decision moved the alliance from paper to posture. The threat is the missiles and the drones fired at Saudi cities and infrastructure.

On Monday, as the delegations met in Tehran, the Houthis claimed fresh strikes on Riyadh airport and the East-West pipeline, claims Saudi Arabia has not confirmed and which remain unverified. Egypt’s parliament the same day authorised military support for the Kingdom.

Washington has raised no objection. Asked about Turkish and Pakistani deployments, President Donald Trump said: “I think they want to help Saudi Arabia, and I think that’s good.” An alliance that stands behind Riyadh without alarming Washington speaks to anyone with authority.

Iran’s position

Iran’s posture is the other half of the equation. In August, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said: “We have not received a formal invitation [to join the alliance], but proposals have been raised for dialogue with these countries on matters related to collective security in the region.” Formal membership is not realistic: Tehran’s preference for “security originating from within the region” implies an order without American forces, which the signatories do not necessarily share. But structured dialogue is realistic, and it is precisely what Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye carried to Tehran.

The diplomatic gap between Washington and Tehran remains wide. The US wants enrichment curbed and IAEA inspectors back; Iran wants the naval blockade lifted and a return to the June memorandum of understanding.

An Iranian official told Iran International that nuclear issues would not be discussed until Tehran’s demands were met. Two unnamed US officials said that forces could strike “within 96 hours” of an order. The US midterm elections fall on November 3. The window for diplomacy is narrow, and it is closing.

That is why the Tehran meeting deserves more credit than its modest outcome — an agreement to keep talking — suggests. A senior Pakistani security official said the aim was “a regional non-aggression network.” Pakistan brought Riyadh, Ankara and Tehran to the same table at a moment of acute danger, as the Kingdom’s defence partner, not a bystander.

What next?

First, the alliance should resource its defensive tasks: air and missile defence, intelligence sharing and rotational presence to protect the Kingdom from attacks by non-state actors. Egypt, whose foreign minister says accession is under “serious consideration”, should be welcomed on the same terms.

Second, a non-aggression track with Iran should run beside the alliance, not inside it, so that dialogue never dilutes deterrence. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Qatar are well placed to act as its guarantors and facilitators. Regular contact among defence and security chiefs would lower the risk of miscalculation in the Gulf and in Yemen.

Third, Pakistan should keep its channels credible in both capitals. Its value to Washington and to Tehran lies in being trusted by each, and its commitment to Saudi Arabia rests on the Kingdom’s security. Pakistan shares a long border with Iran and a deep bond with Gulf; its stake in the stability of both flanks is matched by its resolve to stand by its partners.

Islamabad’s course, then, is to keep its treaty commitments firm and its deterrence credible, so that restraint is never mistaken for hesitation, while strengthening the confidence of Riyadh and Ankara and the security of Pakistan’s western frontier.

That is what Field Marshal Munir’s presence in Tehran signalled: Pakistan stands with the Kingdom, and the path away from escalation runs through respect for its security. For Pakistan, diplomacy backed by deterrence is strategy at its most disciplined. The lasting measure of power is not only the wars a state can fight, but the wars its strength and judgement deter.

headline: 'Over a million' abuse images found on phone of UK man who drugged, raped wife: prosecutor
description: Court hears trial of nine men accused of various sexual offences against a woman who was abused by her husband.
author: AFP
article_text:
A man who drugged and raped his wife over two decades and allegedly invited strangers to participate had “over a million photographs and videos” on his phone cataloguing the abuse, a UK court heard on Monday.

The court in Manchester, northwest England, is hearing the trial of nine men accused of various sexual offences against a woman who was abused by her husband — a man in his 60s who cannot be named to protect the victim’s identity.

The husband filmed and shared images of the abuse on the “internet and social media applications” with “other like-minded men”, prosecutor Louise Oakley told the court.

Some of the defendants allegedly “hid behind a screen” and conspired with the husband over the years to administer substances to the woman so she could be “used and abused”.

And starting 2023, the prosecutor said, the husband began inviting men around to their home and filmed himself and others raping her while she was unconscious.

It is the second case involving a man accused of inviting strangers to take part in abusing his wife currently being heard in Britain. A trial in Winchester in the south involving four men opened last week.

Global awareness of the crime, known as organised drug-facilitated sexual assault (DFSA), has grown following the high-profile conviction in France of Dominique Pelicot, who drugged and raped his then-wife Gisele for nearly a decade alongside strangers.

Oakley told the jury in Manchester that the husband’s phone, which was seized when he was arrested, was like a “confession booth” including “barbaric sexual fantasies” going back to 2004.

“There were over a million photographs and videos cataloguing not only his abuse of his wife but abuse on her committed by others, including those in the dock today,” Oakley said.

“There is no doubt he lived a double life masked in respectability,” the prosecutor said.

The husband pleaded guilty in September to some 60 sexual offences against his wife, including administering a substance with intent to stupefy or overpower her.

He and 13 other men are accused of conspiring to abuse the woman. Four of the men have since pleaded guilty to various offences.

The remaining nine men, aged between 28 and 70, deny various charges including rape, sexual assault and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

They include a taxi driver, a recruitment agency worker, a building supplies worker and a senior medic.

headline: Govt slashes high-speed diesel price by Rs7.76 per litre, petrol by Rs3.40
description: Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs374.51 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs395.20.
author: News Desk
article_text:
The government on Monday slashed the price of petrol by Rs3.40 per litre, and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs7.76.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs374.51 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs395.20.

The prices are applicable for Nov 3 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

However, under a new arrangement, oil refineries would contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a monthly cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This would allow a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price on consumers’ end.

“The [petroleum levy] impact on estimated total country volume of Rs. 14.71/litre shall be surrendered by refineries @ Rs49.02/litre on their sales to [oil marketing companies],” reads a document by Ogra.

The government announced the arrangement during a press conference in Islamabad, held by Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar.

“I am grateful to all the refineries that saw the public is in difficulty and with the government’s help … increased their throughput,” Malik said, adding that these refineries had made profits from this throughput in the last three months.

“They were requested to take a step to support the public during this difficult time, and I am glad that they listened to us … the Rs15 increase that was coming in the petrol prices on Friday, they helped the government with that. Because of that, we were able to maintain the price.”

On Oct 27, Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman met with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad to discuss his party’s demand to provide relief to the public by abolishing the levy.

The two sides agreed to form a joint committee of the JI and the government to consider the expansion of the ongoing fuel relief scheme, being offered to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc since Sept 17.

For his part, Rehman declared that his party would march to Islamabad in protest of the petroleum levy in mid-November if the government did not announce any major relief by then.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50 per cent for three months.

On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

article_html:
The government on Monday slashed the price of petrol by Rs3.40 per litre, and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs7.76.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs374.51 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs395.20.

The prices are applicable for Nov 3 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

However, under a new arrangement, oil refineries would contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a monthly cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This would allow a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price on consumers’ end.

“The [petroleum levy] impact on estimated total country volume of Rs. 14.71/litre shall be surrendered by refineries @ Rs49.02/litre on their sales to [oil marketing companies],” reads a document by Ogra.

The government announced the arrangement during a press conference in Islamabad, held by Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar.

“I am grateful to all the refineries that saw the public is in difficulty and with the government’s help … increased their throughput,” Malik said, adding that these refineries had made profits from this throughput in the last three months.

“They were requested to take a step to support the public during this difficult time, and I am glad that they listened to us … the Rs15 increase that was coming in the petrol prices on Friday, they helped the government with that. Because of that, we were able to maintain the price.”

On Oct 27, Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman met with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad to discuss his party’s demand to provide relief to the public by abolishing the levy.

The two sides agreed to form a joint committee of the JI and the government to consider the expansion of the ongoing fuel relief scheme, being offered to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc since Sept 17.

For his part, Rehman declared that his party would march to Islamabad in protest of the petroleum levy in mid-November if the government did not announce any major relief by then.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50 per cent for three months.

On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

headline: Trump touts Washington reflecting pool as US midterm battle reaches finale
description: Polls show Democrats poised to seize the House of Representatives and within reach of the Senate in Tuesday’s vote.
author: Reuters, AFP
article_text:
United States President Donald Trump devoted his final public remarks before Tuesday’s midterm elections to touting renovations of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, even as Democrats sought to contain a rift in Michigan’s closely fought US Senate race.

Polls show Democrats poised to seize the House of Representatives and within reach of the Senate in Tuesday’s vote — a shift that would impose tight political constraints on the president.

In his only public remarks scheduled for Monday, Trump — a former real-estate developer — spent more than 20 minutes discussing pipes, joints, caulking, granite resurfacing, algae and leaks at the belated reopening of the Washington reflecting pool.

“Does somebody have those pictures for me?” the president asked his aides before sharing illustrations of the “miles of joints” that had been replaced.

“So we have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that you don’t have enough time,” Trump said, also mentioning the grass at the White House, his new Marine One helipad, a golf course and a triumphal arch that faces a court challenge.

He made brief reference to the election, saying: “When you vote, remember: a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country.”

A White House official earlier told AFP that the speech would highlight “this administration’s achievements to make the country safer and wealthier” while contrasting “the Republicans’ commonsense America First agenda” with “the Democrats’ radical, America Last agenda”.

The pool — an iconic landmark where botched repairs came to symbolise the 80-year-old’s chaotic presidency — is one of the US capital’s historic stages. Martin Luther King delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech in 1963 from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, overlooking the pool.

Trump said on Sunday he picked the site “just to show how beautiful it is”. But the roughly $15 million renovation left the pool’s lining peeling and its water green with algae. He pointed at vandalism, but federal prosecutors blamed faulty work.

Under Trump, it has also become part of a sweeping drive to remake Washington, which has included tearing down part of the White House and threatening to demolish the city’s premier arts centre.

Trump has predicted victory in the midterms for his Republicans, but he acknowledged the alternative in an interview released on Monday by the New York Post’s Pod Force One podcast.

“I think we’re going to do great — but if we didn’t win, I veto everything,” he said. “I’ll be vetoing, vetoing. And then they’ll come along and we’ll probably make some deals along the way.”

Winning just the House would give Democrats voting power over the federal budget and control of committees able to investigate alleged corruption under Trump, the Epstein files and other explosive issues.

A Democratic Senate could also block Trump’s lifetime appointments to the courts, including the Supreme Court.

‘Ransack, rape and plunder’

Trump warned Republican lawmakers in January that losing the midterms would lead to his impeachment.

The loss of total Republican control would push him toward lame-duck status, with high inflation at home and the war against Iran still weighing on his presidency.

Democrats, meanwhile, prepared final rallies in battleground states, including in Texas with James Talarico and in Kansas with Adam Hamilton — two star Senate candidates seeking major upsets. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.

But a decade into the Trump era, Democrats remain wary of predicting victory.

Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock told CNN that the mood was “nauseously optimistic”.

Republicans have run a scorched-earth campaign, painting Democrats as communists and branding Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, a terrorist.

Addressing a crowd in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said Democrats are “extreme and dangerous radicals” who will “steal your wealth” and let in migrants to “ransack, rape and plunder”.

Democrats have faced late divisions of their own, with left-wing candidates at times clashing with the party establishment.

On Sunday, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in Michigan’s pivotal Senate race. Stevens lost a bruising primary to El-Sayed in August despite establishment backing.

Senate in play

While the House appears highly likely to turn Democratic, the battle for the Senate is far closer.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Only a third of the 100 seats are being contested, and few of those races initially looked favorable to the party.

To win, Democrats must flip seats in states that Trump carried by double digits two years ago.

Forecaster Decision Desk HQ has Democrats winning the Senate 52-48 and the House by a comfortable 241-194.

The final New York Times/Siena poll, released Sunday evening, showed Democrats leading in all seven of the most competitive Senate races, though five were within the margin of error.

Tuesday is election day, but a record 54 million people have already cast ballots.

The midterms have also drawn about $11bn in advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.

Elon Musk, the Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE drive to slash the federal government, has given nearly half a billion dollars to help elect Republicans.

Under Trump, it has also become part of a sweeping drive to remake Washington, which has included tearing down part of the White House and threatening to demolish the city’s premier arts centre.

Trump has predicted victory in the midterms for his Republicans, but he acknowledged the alternative in an interview released on Monday by the New York Post’s Pod Force One podcast.

“I think we’re going to do great — but if we didn’t win, I veto everything,” he said. “I’ll be vetoing, vetoing. And then they’ll come along and we’ll probably make some deals along the way.”

Winning just the House would give Democrats voting power over the federal budget and control of committees able to investigate alleged corruption under Trump, the Epstein files and other explosive issues.

A Democratic Senate could also block Trump’s lifetime appointments to the courts, including the Supreme Court.

‘Ransack, rape and plunder’

Trump warned Republican lawmakers in January that losing the midterms would lead to his impeachment.

The loss of total Republican control would push him toward lame-duck status, with high inflation at home and the war against Iran still weighing on his presidency.

Democrats, meanwhile, prepared final rallies in battleground states, including in Texas with James Talarico and in Kansas with Adam Hamilton — two star Senate candidates seeking major upsets. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.

But a decade into the Trump era, Democrats remain wary of predicting victory.

Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock told CNN that the mood was “nauseously optimistic”.

Republicans have run a scorched-earth campaign, painting Democrats as communists and branding Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, a terrorist.

Addressing a crowd in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said Democrats are “extreme and dangerous radicals” who will “steal your wealth” and let in migrants to “ransack, rape and plunder”.

Democrats have faced late divisions of their own, with left-wing candidates at times clashing with the party establishment.

On Sunday, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in Michigan’s pivotal Senate race. Stevens lost a bruising primary to El-Sayed in August despite establishment backing.

Senate in play

While the House appears highly likely to turn Democratic, the battle for the Senate is far closer.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Only a third of the 100 seats are being contested, and few of those races initially looked favorable to the party.

To win, Democrats must flip seats in states that Trump carried by double digits two years ago.

Forecaster Decision Desk HQ has Democrats winning the Senate 52-48 and the House by a comfortable 241-194.

The final New York Times/Siena poll, released Sunday evening, showed Democrats leading in all seven of the most competitive Senate races, though five were within the margin of error.

Tuesday is election day, but a record 54 million people have already cast ballots.

The midterms have also drawn about $11bn in advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.

Elon Musk, the Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE drive to slash the federal government, has given nearly half a billion dollars to help elect Republicans.
